docs.title: Additory
docs.text:
Elegant data operations for DataFrames. Lookup, transform, generate, compare — all through a consistent, expressive API.

v0.1.3a11

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install additory

Requires Python 3.9+. Works with both polars (required) and pandas (optional).

docs.title: :material-table-arrow-left: add.to() — Bring data from one DataFrame to another
docs.text:
Look up columns from a reference table and attach them to your target DataFrame. Supports aggregation, multi-key joins, and list-of-DataFrames patterns.

import additory as add

result = add.to(patients, bring_from=doctors, bring='name', against='doctor_id')

Learn more :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: :material-swap-horizontal: add.transform() — Reshape data in place
docs.text:
Twelve modes for calculating, filtering, sorting, aggregating, deducing, encoding, and more — all through a single function.

result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity', name='total')

Learn more :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: :material-flask-outline: add.synthetic() — Generate realistic data
docs.text:
Create new DataFrames from scratch or augment existing ones with synthetic rows. Pipe-friendly.

result = add.synthetic(df, n=500)
result = df.pipe(add.synthetic, n=500)

Learn more :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: :material-magnify: add.scan() — Inspect and compare
docs.text:
Analyze data quality, track lineage, and compare DataFrames with @diff.

add.scan('@analyze', df)
add.scan('@diff', old=df_jan, new=df_feb)

Learn more :material-arrow-right: · Diff :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: :material-function-variant: add.<dynamic>() — Call expressions by name
docs.text:
Load named expressions from .add files and call them directly on the module.

add.scan('@set', './my_expressions')
result = add.bmi(df)

Learn more :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Pipe Compatibility
docs.text:
Some functions work with df.pipe() for fluent method chaining. add.to(), add.synthetic(), and add.<dynamic>() are pipe-friendly. add.transform() and add.scan() are not (their first argument is a mode string, not a DataFrame).

docs.text:
Track data provenance across operations with lineage=True. View the full operation history, column sources, and row mappings with add.scan('@lineage', df). Session-only by design — lineage lives in memory and is never written to disk.

docs.title: Type Handling
docs.text:
Additory works with both pandas and polars DataFrames. Output type matches input type by default. Use as_type to force a specific output type. Polars is the native internal format; pandas inputs are converted via Arrow IPC.

docs.title: Lineage Tracking
docs.text: Track how your data was transformed — which columns came from where, which rows were filtered, and what operations were applied. Lineage is session-only by design: it lives in memory and is never written to disk.

docs.title: Enabling Lineage
docs.text:
Pass lineage=True to any core function:

import additory as add
import polars as pl

orders = pl.DataFrame({
    'order_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'customer_id': [101, 102, 101],
    'amount': [100, 200, 150],
})

customers = pl.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [101, 102],
    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob'],
})

result = add.to(orders, customers, 'name', 'customer_id', lineage=True)

Lineage metadata is attached to the resulting DataFrame and carries forward through subsequent operations.

docs.title: Viewing Lineage
docs.text:
Use add.scan('@lineage', df) to inspect the lineage report:

report = add.scan('@lineage', result)
print(report)

The report shows:

  • Operation history — each transformation in order
  • Column sources — where each column originated
  • Row mapping — how rows were filtered or aggregated

docs.title: Chaining Operations
docs.text:
Lineage accumulates across multiple operations:

# Step 1: Bring data
df = add.to(orders, customers, 'name', 'customer_id', lineage=True)

# Step 2: Calculate
df = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='amount * 1.1', name='total', lineage=True)

# Step 3: Filter
df = add.transform('@filter', df, where='total > 150', lineage=True)

# View complete history
report = add.scan('@lineage', df)
# Shows all 3 operations, column sources, and row transformations

docs.title: Column Sources
docs.text:
For each column in the result, lineage records its origin:

  • Original — column existed in the input DataFrame
  • Brought — column was added via add.to() from a reference DataFrame
  • Calculated — column was created by add.transform('@calc', ...)
  • Synthetic — column was generated by add.synthetic()

docs.title: Row Mapping
docs.text:
Lineage tracks how the row count changes:

  • Filtering — which rows were excluded and why
  • Aggregation — how rows were grouped
  • Synthetic augmentation — how many rows were added

docs.title: Supported Functions
docs.text: Function Lineage Support add.to() ✅ add.transform() ✅ add.synthetic() ✅ add.scan() — (reads lineage, doesn't produce it)

docs.title: Session-Only Storage
docs.text:
Lineage metadata is stored in the DataFrame's native format (as DataFrame attributes). It is:

  • ✅ Preserved when passing DataFrames between additory operations
  • ❌ Lost when saving to CSV, Parquet, or other file formats
  • ❌ Lost when converting between pandas and polars

This is intentional — additory follows a "no file I/O" philosophy. Lineage is a development and debugging tool, not a persistence layer.

docs.title: Mutual Exclusion with as_type
docs.text:
lineage=True and as_type cannot be used together:

# This raises ValueError
result = add.to(orders, customers, 'name', 'customer_id',
    lineage=True, as_type='polars')

The reason: as_type converts the DataFrame to a different type, which would strip the lineage metadata. If you need both, track lineage first, then convert separately:

# Track lineage
result = add.to(orders, customers, 'name', 'customer_id', lineage=True)

# Convert separately (lineage is lost)
result_polars = pl.from_pandas(result)

Lineage is lost on type conversion

Converting a DataFrame with as_type or manually (e.g., pl.from_pandas()) strips lineage metadata. View the lineage report before converting.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Lineage tracking adds minimal overhead:

  • Less than 3ms per operation
  • No significant impact on large DataFrames (tested with 10,000+ rows)
  • Memory overhead is proportional to the number of operations, not the data size

docs.title: Logging & Timing
docs.text: Monitor what additory is doing under the hood with operation logging and performance timing.

docs.title: Operation Logging
docs.text:
Pass logging=True to any core function to see detailed operation logs:

import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'price': [100, 200, 300],
    'quantity': [2, 3, 1],
})

result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity',
    name='total', logging=True)

This prints log messages showing:

  • Function entry point and parameters
  • Validation steps
  • Rust operation calls
  • Data conversion steps

Logging uses Python's standard logging module at the INFO level.

docs.title: Performance Timing
docs.text:
Set the ADDITORY_TIMING environment variable to get a detailed timing breakdown:

ShellPython 
export ADDITORY_TIMING=true
python my_script.py

import os
os.environ['ADDITORY_TIMING'] = 'true'

import additory as add
# ... your code here

When enabled, each operation prints a timing breakdown:

======================================================================
ADDITORY TIMING BREAKDOWN (add.to)
======================================================================
  Arrow encode (ref):        0.12 ms
  Arrow encode (target):     0.08 ms
  Rust operation:            1.45 ms  ← Main operation
  Arrow decode:              0.09 ms
  ─────────────────────────────────
  Total:                     1.74 ms

  Rust operation: 83.3% of total time
  Arrow IPC:      16.7% of total time
======================================================================

This helps identify whether time is spent in:

  • Arrow IPC encoding/decoding — converting between Python DataFrames and Rust
  • Rust operation — the actual computation
  • Python overhead — validation, lineage tracking, type conversion

docs.title: Pipe Compatibility
docs.text: Some additory functions work with df.pipe() for fluent method chaining. Others require a different calling pattern.

docs.title: Which Functions Are Pipe-Friendly?
docs.text: Function Pipe-Friendly Reason add.to() ✅ First argument is a DataFrame (bring_to) add.synthetic() ✅ First argument accepts a DataFrame (df_or_mode) add.<dynamic>() ✅ First argument is a DataFrame add.transform() ❌ First argument is mode (a string) add.scan() ❌ First argument is mode (a string)

docs.title: add.to()
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

patients = pl.DataFrame({
    'patient_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'doctor_id': [101, 102, 101],
})

doctors = pl.DataFrame({
    'doctor_id': [101, 102],
    'name': ['Dr. Sharma', 'Dr. Tanaka'],
})

# Standard call
result = add.to(patients, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id')

# Pipe call — patients flows in as the first argument
result = patients.pipe(add.to, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id')

Chain multiple lookups:

departments = pl.DataFrame({
    'doctor_id': [101, 102],
    'department': ['Cardiology', 'Orthopedics'],
})

result = (
    patients
    .pipe(add.to, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id')
    .pipe(add.to, departments, 'department', 'doctor_id')
)

docs.title: add.synthetic()
docs.text:
In augment mode, the first argument is a DataFrame:

df = pl.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3], 'y': [4, 5, 6]})

# Standard call
result = add.synthetic(df, n=100)

# Pipe call
result = df.pipe(add.synthetic, n=100)

docs.title: add.\<dynamic>()
docs.text:
Dynamic functions take a DataFrame as the first argument:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'weight': [70, 85, 60],
    'height': [1.70, 1.80, 1.65],
})

# Standard call
result = add.bmi(df)

# Pipe call
result = df.pipe(add.bmi)

docs.title: Why add.transform() Is Not Pipe-Friendly
docs.text:
add.transform() takes mode as its first argument:

# mode is the first argument, not a DataFrame
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='x * 2', name='x2')

Since df.pipe() passes the DataFrame as the first argument, it would collide with the mode parameter. Use add.transform() as a standalone call instead.

Workaround with a lambda

If you really want chaining, wrap the call: 

result = (
    df
    .pipe(lambda d: add.transform('@calc', d, expression='x * 2', name='x2'))
    .pipe(lambda d: add.transform('@filter', d, where='x2 > 4'))
)
This works but is less readable than sequential calls.

docs.title: Why add.scan() Is Not Pipe-Friendly
docs.text:
Same reason — mode is the first argument:

result = add.scan('@analyze', df)

Use it as a standalone call.

docs.title: Practical Pattern
docs.text:
Combine pipe-friendly and standalone calls in a workflow:

import additory as add
import polars as pl

# Pipe-friendly chain
enriched = (
    orders
    .pipe(add.to, customers, 'name', 'customer_id')
    .pipe(add.to, products, 'price', 'product_id')
)

# Standalone transform calls
result = add.transform('@calc', enriched, expression='price * quantity', name='total')
result = add.transform('@filter', result, where='total > 100')
result = add.transform('@sort', result, by='total', strategy='desc')

docs.title: Type Handling
docs.text: Additory works with both pandas and polars DataFrames. By default, the output type matches the input type. Use as_type to override this behaviour.

docs.title: Default Behaviour
docs.text:
Pass in a pandas DataFrame, get a pandas DataFrame back. Same for polars:

PolarsPandas 
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3]})
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='x * 2', name='x2')
type(result)  # polars.DataFrame

import additory as add
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3]})
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='x * 2', name='x2')
type(result)  # pandas.DataFrame

docs.title: The as_type Parameter
docs.text:
Force the output to a specific type regardless of input:

import additory as add
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3]})

# Input is pandas, but force polars output
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='x * 2', name='x2', as_type='polars')
type(result)  # polars.DataFrame
as_type Value Output Type None (default) Same as input 'pandas' pandas.DataFrame 'polars' polars.DataFrame

docs.title: Supported Functions
docs.text: Function as_type Support add.to() ✅ add.transform() ✅ add.synthetic() ✅ add.scan() ✅ (also supports 'dict' and 'text')

docs.title: Internal Processing
docs.text:
Internally, additory converts all DataFrames to polars for processing in Rust, then converts back to the target type. This means:

  • Polars input → no conversion overhead (native format)
  • Pandas input → converted to polars via Arrow IPC, processed, converted back

Polars is faster

If performance matters, use polars DataFrames directly to avoid the pandas↔polars conversion overhead. The conversion is fast (sub-millisecond for small DataFrames) but adds up in tight loops.

docs.title: Type Preservation
docs.text:
Additory preserves column data types through operations:

  • Integer columns stay integer (unless the operation produces floats)
  • String columns stay string
  • Datetime columns stay datetime
  • Null values are preserved as native null types

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Library Status Notes polars Required Core dependency, always available pyarrow Required Needed for DataFrame serialization pandas Optional Install with pip install additory[pandas] or pip install pandas

If pandas is not installed and you pass as_type='pandas', additory raises an ImportError with a helpful message.

docs.title: Mutual Exclusion with Lineage
docs.text:
as_type cannot be used together with lineage=True. Lineage metadata is stored in the DataFrame's native format and would be lost during type conversion. See Lineage Tracking for details.

# This raises ValueError
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', lineage=True, as_type='polars')

docs.title: Core Functions
docs.text: Additory provides five core functions plus a dynamic expression API. Each function handles a distinct category of DataFrame operations.

docs.title: add.to()
docs.text:
Bring columns from one DataFrame into another by matching on a key column. Supports lookups, joins, aggregation strategies, and list-of-DataFrames patterns.

result = add.to(orders, customers, 'name', 'customer_id')

→ Full documentation

docs.title: add.transform()
docs.text:
Transform data within a single DataFrame using one of 12 modes — calculate, filter, sort, aggregate, encode, impute, and more.

result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity', name='total')

→ Full documentation · Transform Modes

docs.title: add.synthetic()
docs.text:
Generate synthetic data from scratch or augment existing DataFrames with realistic rows.

result = add.synthetic('@new', n=1000, strategy={'age': 'normal(40, 10)'})

→ Full documentation

docs.title: add.scan()
docs.text:
Inspect, analyze, and compare DataFrames. Covers statistical profiling, lineage reports, diff comparison, and expression management.

result = add.scan('@analyze', df)

→ Full documentation · Diff documentation

docs.title: add.\<dynamic>()
docs.text:
Call named expressions as functions. Any expression registered in the expression registry becomes a callable on the add module.

docs.title: add.scan('@diff')

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description mode str (required) Must be '@diff' old DataFrame (required) The baseline (previous) DataFrame new DataFrame (required) The updated (current) DataFrame key str or list[str] None Key column(s) for row matching. Auto-detected if omitted. columns str or list[str] None Limit comparison to specific columns strategy dict None Diff options: output, exclude, carry, aliases, groups logging bool False Enable detailed operation logging as_type str None Force output type: 'pandas' or 'polars'

Signature

add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new, *, key=None,
         columns=None, strategy=None, logging=False, as_type=None)

docs.title: Summary Mode (default)
docs.text:
Summary mode produces one row per original row with inline change markers and a _diff_status column:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new)

Each row gets a _diff_status value:

Status Meaning added Row exists only in new removed Row exists only in old modified Row exists in both but values changed no_change Row is identical in both

For modified rows, changed cells show inline markers: "old_value → new_value".

docs.title: Detail Mode
docs.text:
Detail mode produces one row per changed cell, giving granular visibility into every modification:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'output': 'detail'},
)

Detail output columns:

Column Description _key The key value identifying the row _column The column that changed _old_value Value in the old DataFrame _new_value Value in the new DataFrame

docs.title: Auto Key Detection
docs.text:
When key is not specified, the diff engine automatically detects the best key column(s) by looking for:

  1. Columns with all unique values (candidate primary keys)
  2. Columns with names suggesting identity (*_id, *_key, *_code)
  3. The column with the highest cardinality ratio
# Auto-detect key
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new)

# Explicit key
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new, key='employee_id')

# Composite key
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new, key=['region', 'product_id'])

Explicit keys are faster

Auto-detection works well for most datasets, but specifying key explicitly skips the detection step and avoids ambiguity.

docs.title: Duplicate Handling
docs.text:
When the key column contains duplicate values, the diff engine flags them rather than producing incorrect comparisons:

# If old_df has duplicate keys, they appear in the output
# with _diff_status = 'duplicate'
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new)

Duplicates are reported separately so you can clean the data before re-running the diff.

docs.title: Strategy Options
docs.text:
The strategy dictionary controls diff behaviour:

Key Type Default Description output str 'summary' Output mode: 'summary' or 'detail' exclude list[str] [] Columns to ignore during comparison carry list[str] [] Extra columns to include in output (not compared) aliases dict or str None Column value aliases for case-insensitive matching groups str None Reconciliation group name for hierarchical comparison

docs.title: Excluding columns
docs.text:
Skip volatile columns (timestamps, auto-generated IDs) that would create noise:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'exclude': ['updated_at', 'row_hash']},
)

docs.title: Carrying extra columns
docs.text:
Include columns in the output for context without comparing them:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'carry': ['created_by', 'notes']},
)

docs.title: Reconciliation
docs.text: For advanced comparisons, use reconciliation .add files to define aliases and groups.

docs.title: Aliases — Case-insensitive variant matching
docs.text:
Aliases map variant spellings to a canonical form before comparison:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={
        'aliases': {
            'status': ['Active', 'ACTIVE', 'active'],
            'region': ['NA', 'North America'],
        },
    },
)

Or load aliases from a registered reconciliation file:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'aliases': 'my_reconciliation'},
)

docs.title: Groups — Hierarchical change detection
docs.text:
Groups define column hierarchies for structured change detection. Load them from a reconciliation .add file:

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'groups': 'my_reconciliation'},
)

See the Reconciliation Guide for the full .add file format.

docs.title: How It Works — __getattr__ Resolution
docs.text:
When you call add.bmi(df), Python's attribute lookup triggers __getattr__('bmi') on the additory module. The resolution chain:

  1. Check if bmi is a reserved name (built-in function) — if so, return the built-in
  2. Look up bmi in the expression registry
  3. If found, create a dynamic function that applies the expression to the DataFrame
  4. If not found, raise AttributeError
# These are equivalent:
result = add.bmi(df)
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='weight / (height ** 2)', name='bmi')

The dynamic API is syntactic sugar over add.transform('@calc', ...).

docs.title: .add File Format
docs.text:
Expressions are defined in .add files using TOML syntax. Each expression is a top-level table:

[bmi]
expression = "weight / (height ** 2)"
category = "medical"

[revenue]
expression = "price * quantity"
category = "finance"

[margin]
expression = "(revenue - cost) / revenue * 100"
category = "finance"
Field Required Description expression Yes The calculation formula category No Grouping category for organization

Save this as my_expressions.add in a folder, then load it:

add.scan('@set', './expressions_folder')

See the Expression Files Guide for the complete format reference.

docs.title: Column Auto-Matching
docs.text:
When you call add.bmi(df), additory inspects the expression weight / (height ** 2) and looks for columns named weight and height in the DataFrame. If they exist, they are used automatically.

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'weight': [70, 80, 65],
    'height': [1.75, 1.80, 1.60],
})

# Columns match the expression variables — auto-matched
result = add.bmi(df)

docs.title: Explicit Column Mapping
docs.text:
When DataFrame columns have different names, use keyword arguments to map them:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'body_weight': [70, 80, 65],
    'body_height': [1.75, 1.80, 1.60],
})

# Map expression variables to actual column names
result = add.bmi(df, weight='body_weight', height='body_height')

docs.title: Loading from a folder
docs.text:
# Load all .add files from a folder
add.scan('@set', './my_expressions')

This scans the folder for .add files and registers all expressions found.

docs.title: Viewing loaded expressions
docs.text:

docs.title: Reserved Names
docs.text:
The following names are reserved for built-in functions and cannot be used as expression names:

Reserved Name Built-in Function to add.to() synthetic add.synthetic() scan add.scan() transform add.transform() harmonize add.transform('@harmonize', ...)

If an expression file defines a name that conflicts with a reserved name, the built-in function takes precedence.

Name collisions

If you name an expression to or scan, it will be silently ignored. Choose descriptive names like calculate_bmi or compute_revenue to avoid conflicts.

    df
    .pipe(add.bmi)
    .pipe(add.revenue)
    .pipe(add.to, reference, 'name', 'id')

docs.title: add.scan()
docs.text: Inspect, analyze, and explain DataFrames. add.scan() is the read-only counterpart to the other core functions — it never modifies data, only reports on it.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', None],
    'age': [28, 35, None, 42],
    'salary': [55000, 72000, 61000, 48000],
})

report = add.scan('@analyze', df)
print(report)

The first argument is the mode — a string starting with @ that selects the scan operation.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description mode str (required) Scan mode: '@analyze', '@analyse', '@lineage', '@diff', or '@set' df DataFrame or str None Input DataFrame, or a path string for @set mode columns str or list[str] None Limit analysis to specific columns where str None SQL-like filter condition applied before analysis rows str or list[str] None Row range specifications trace list[int] None [col_idx, row_idx] for cell-level tracing focus str None Specialized analysis mode as_type str None Output format: 'pandas', 'polars', 'dict', or 'text' old DataFrame None Baseline DataFrame (for @diff mode) new DataFrame None Updated DataFrame (for @diff mode) key str or list[str] None Key column(s) for @diff mode strategy dict None Options for @diff mode logging bool False Enable detailed operation logging

Signature

add.scan(mode, df=None, *, old=None, new=None, key=None,
         columns=None, where=None, rows=None, trace=None,
         focus=None, strategy=None, logging=False, as_type=None)

docs.title: Modes
docs.text: Mode Purpose Requires df Details @analyze Statistical profiling Yes Data types, nulls, distributions, quality metrics @analyse Same as @analyze (British spelling) Yes Alias for @analyze @lineage Transformation history Yes Requires lineage=True on prior operations @diff Compare two DataFrames No (old/new instead) See add.scan('@diff') @set Load expression files No (path string instead) See add.<dynamic>()

Produces a statistical profile of the DataFrame including data types, null counts, unique values, and distribution summaries.

docs.title: @lineage — Transformation History
docs.text:
View the chain of operations that produced a DataFrame. Lineage tracking must be enabled on prior operations by passing lineage=True.

# Enable lineage on operations
result = add.to(patients, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id', lineage=True)
result = add.transform('@calc', result, expression='1', name='flag', lineage=True)

# View the lineage
lineage = add.scan('@lineage', result)
print(lineage)

docs.title: What lineage tracks
docs.text: Tracked Item Description Operation type Which function was called (add.to, add.transform, add.synthetic) Parameters The arguments passed to each operation Row counts Rows before and after each operation Column changes Columns added or modified by each operation Column sources Which operation produced each column

docs.title: Enabling lineage
docs.text:
Pass lineage=True to any core function:

result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', lineage=True)
result = add.transform('@calc', result, expression='price * qty', name='total', lineage=True)
result = add.synthetic(result, n=100, lineage=True)

Lineage accumulates across operations — each step appends to the history.

Lineage requires prior tracking

Calling add.scan('@lineage', df) on a DataFrame without lineage metadata raises a ValueError. Make sure at least one prior operation used lineage=True.

Lineage and as_type are mutually exclusive

You cannot use lineage=True and as_type together on the same operation. Lineage metadata is stored in the DataFrame's native format and would be lost during type conversion. Convert the type separately after tracking lineage.

print(path)

@set does not accept a DataFrame

Unlike other scan modes, @set takes a path string as its second argument, not a DataFrame.

See the Expression Files Guide for the complete .add file format, and add.<dynamic>() for using loaded expressions.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description bring_to DataFrame or list[DataFrame] (required) Target DataFrame(s) to add columns to bring_from DataFrame or list[DataFrame] (required) Reference DataFrame(s) to look up from bring str or list[str] (required) Column name(s) to bring from the reference against str or list[str] (required) Key column(s) to match on position str or int None Where to place new columns: 'start', 'end', 'after:col', 'before:col', or integer index strategy dict None Column-level aggregation strategies (e.g., {'amount': 'sum'}) join_type str 'lookup' Join type: 'lookup', 'left', 'inner', 'outer' logging bool False Enable detailed operation logging lineage bool False Enable lineage tracking as_type str None Force output type: 'pandas' or 'polars'

Signature

add.to(bring_to, bring_from, bring, against, position=None, *,
       strategy=None, join_type='lookup', logging=False,
       lineage=False, as_type=None)

docs.title: Join Types
docs.text:
The join_type parameter controls how rows are matched:

Join Type Behaviour 'lookup' Default. Brings columns from the reference where keys match. Unmatched rows in the target keep null values. 'left' Standard left join — all target rows preserved. 'inner' Only rows with matching keys in both DataFrames. 'outer' All rows from both DataFrames, with null where no match exists. 
# Inner join — only matched rows
result = add.to(patients, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id', join_type='inner')

docs.title: Aggregation Strategies
docs.text:
When the reference has multiple rows per key, use strategy to control how values are combined:

result = add.to(
    customers,
    orders,
    'amount',
    'customer_id',
    strategy={'amount': 'sum'},
)

Available aggregation strategies:

Strategy Description 'sum' Sum of values 'count' Count of values 'average' Mean of values 'min' Minimum value 'max' Maximum value 'concat' Concatenate text values 'most_common' Most frequent value 'least_common' Least frequent value 'median' Median value 'std' Standard deviation 'variance' Variance 'unique_count' Count of distinct values

docs.title: List-of-DataFrames Patterns
docs.text:
add.to() supports passing lists of DataFrames for batch operations:

# One-to-many: single target, multiple references
result = add.to(
    customers,
    [orders_jan, orders_feb, orders_mar],
    'amount',
    'customer_id',
    strategy={'amount': 'sum'},
)

# Many-to-one: multiple targets, single reference
results = add.to(
    [customers_a, customers_b],
    products,
    'product_name',
    'product_id',
)
# results is a list of DataFrames

When bring_from is a list, the references are concatenated vertically before the lookup. When bring_to is a list, each target is processed independently and a list of results is returned.

# Place at the start
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', position='start')

# Place after a specific column
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', position='after:email')

# Place before a specific column
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', position='before:status')

# Place at a specific index
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', position=2)

    patients
    .pipe(add.to, doctors, 'name', 'doctor_id')

Parameter Type Default Description mode str (required) Transform mode (e.g., '@calc', '@filter', '@sort') df DataFrame (required) Input DataFrame to transform columns str or list[str] None Column(s) to transform or select expression str or list[str] None Expression(s) to evaluate (for @calc) where str None Filter condition (for @filter) by str or list[str] None Grouping or sorting column(s) name str or list[str] None Output column name(s) for calculated results order str None Sort order: 'asc' or 'desc' position str or int 'end' Where to place new columns strategy str or dict None Mode-specific options infer str or list[str] None Column(s) to impute (for @deduce) against str or list[str] None Text column(s) for TF-IDF similarity (for @deduce) method str or list[str] None Imputation method (for @deduce) logging bool False Enable detailed operation logging lineage bool False Enable lineage tracking as_type str None Force output type: 'pandas' or 'polars'

add.transform(mode, df, columns=None, *, expression=None, where=None,
              by=None, name=None, order=None, position='end',

              logging=False, lineage=False, as_type=None)

docs.title: All 12 Modes
docs.text: Mode Purpose Key Parameters Details @calc Calculate new columns expression, name, strategy Arithmetic, string ops, built-in expressions @filter Filter rows where, columns SQL-like conditions @sort Sort rows by, strategy Ascending/descending @aggregate Group and summarize by, strategy sum, count, average, min, max, and more @harmonize Unit conversions columns, strategy Weight, length, temperature, and more @round Round numeric values columns, strategy Banker's rounding @transpose Transpose DataFrame — Swap rows and columns @extract Extract patterns columns, expression Regex and datetime extraction @split Split text columns columns, by Split into multiple columns @onehot One-hot encoding columns Binary indicator columns @label Label encoding columns Numeric category labels @deduce Impute missing values infer, method, against mean, median, knn, TF-IDF

docs.title: pandas support
docs.text:
additory works with both polars and pandas DataFrames. If you want to pass pandas DataFrames directly:

pip install pandas

When you pass a pandas DataFrame, additory converts it to polars internally, performs the operation, and converts the result back to pandas. You can override this with the as_type parameter on any function.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
import additory as add
print(add.__version__)
# 0.1.3a11

Check that the Rust bindings loaded:

print(add.RUST_AVAILABLE)
# True

If RUST_AVAILABLE is False, only Python-only modes (like @knn imputation) will work. See Troubleshooting for help with Rust binding issues.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
additory's core is written in Rust with Python bindings via PyO3. To build from source you need:

  1. Rust toolchain — install via rustup
  2. maturin — the build tool for PyO3 projects
# Install maturin
pip install maturin

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/sekarkrishna/additory.git
cd additory

# Build and install in development mode
maturin develop --release

For a wheel you can distribute:

maturin build --release
pip install target/wheels/additory-*.whl

Development mode

Use maturin develop (without --release) for faster builds during development. The --release flag enables Rust optimizations and is recommended for benchmarking and production use.

docs.title: Expression Files
docs.text: Expression files (.add files) define named formulas in TOML format. They power the dynamic API (add.<name>(df)) and the inbuilt: prefix in @calc mode.

docs.title: The .add File Format
docs.text:
Each .add file is a TOML file where every top-level table defines one expression:

[bmi]
expression = "weight / (height ** 2)"
description = "Body Mass Index - weight in kg, height in meters"
category = "medical"

[roi]
expression = "((revenue - cost) / cost) * 100"
description = "Return on Investment percentage"
category = "finance"

docs.title: Required Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description expression string The formula to evaluate. Column names become variables. description string Human-readable description of the expression category string Category for organization (e.g., "finance", "medical")

docs.title: Optional Input Definitions
docs.text:
Add an [expression_name.inputs] table to document expected columns:

[bmi]
expression = "weight / (height ** 2)"
description = "Body Mass Index"
category = "medical"

[bmi.inputs]
weight = { type = "numeric", unit = "kg", description = "Body weight" }
height = { type = "numeric", unit = "m", description = "Height" }

Input definitions are used for documentation and validation. They don't change how the expression is evaluated.

docs.title: From a folder
docs.text:
Use add.scan('@set', folder_path) to load all .add files from a directory:

import additory as add

# Load expressions from a folder
add.scan('@set', '/path/to/my/expressions/')

All .add files in the folder are parsed and registered. After loading, expressions are available via the dynamic API:

result = add.bmi(df)
result = add.roi(df)

docs.title: Querying loaded expressions
docs.text:
Use add.scan('@set', 'show') to list all currently registered expressions:

info = add.scan('@set', 'show')
print(info)

docs.title: Writing a Custom .add File
docs.text:
Here's a complete example for a retail analytics team:

retail_metrics.add
[revenue_per_unit]
expression = "total_revenue / units_sold"
description = "Average revenue per unit sold"
category = "retail"

[gross_margin]
expression = "((selling_price - cost_price) / selling_price) * 100"
description = "Gross margin percentage"
category = "retail"

[inventory_turnover]
expression = "cost_of_goods_sold / average_inventory"
description = "Inventory turnover ratio"
category = "retail"

[days_of_supply]
expression = "average_inventory / (cost_of_goods_sold / 365)"
description = "Days of supply remaining"
category = "retail"

Save this as retail_metrics.add in your expressions folder, then load it:

import additory as add
import polars as pl

# Load the custom expressions
add.scan('@set', './my_expressions/')

# Use them
products = pl.DataFrame({
    'product': ['Widget', 'Gadget'],
    'total_revenue': [50000, 80000],
    'units_sold': [1000, 500],
})

result = add.revenue_per_unit(products)
print(result)

docs.title: How Expressions Are Resolved
docs.text:
When you call add.bmi(df), additory:

  1. Looks up "bmi" in the expression registry
  2. Finds the formula: weight / (height ** 2)
  3. Matches column names in the formula to columns in your DataFrame
  4. Evaluates the expression via @calc mode
  5. Returns the DataFrame with the new column

docs.title: Column Auto-Matching
docs.text: The expression's variable names are matched against your DataFrame's column names. If your DataFrame has columns named weight and height, the bmi expression works automatically.

docs.title: Explicit Mapping
docs.text:
If your column names don't match, use keyword arguments:

# DataFrame has 'mass' and 'stature' instead of 'weight' and 'height'
result = add.bmi(df, weight='mass', height='stature')

docs.text:

docs.title: Reserved Names
docs.text:
Some names are reserved and cannot be used as expression names:

  • to, transform, synthetic, scan — core function names
  • analyze, analyse — scan mode aliases
  • play — internal use

If you try to register an expression with a reserved name, additory raises a ValueError.

docs.title: Reconciliation
docs.text: Reconciliation .add files define aliases and groups for add.scan('@diff'). They let you normalize variant spellings before comparison and detect changes at different levels of a column hierarchy.

docs.title: Why Reconciliation?
docs.text:
Real-world data is messy. The same value appears in different forms:

  • "Active", "ACTIVE", "active" — same meaning, different case
  • "North America", "NA", "N. America" — same region, different abbreviations

Without reconciliation, the diff engine flags these as changes. With reconciliation, they're treated as equivalent.

docs.title: Reconciliation .add File Format
docs.text:
A reconciliation .add file uses TOML format with two sections: [aliases] and [groups].

my_reconciliation.add
[aliases]
status = ["Active", "ACTIVE", "active", "Inactive", "INACTIVE", "inactive"]
region = ["NA", "North America", "N. America", "EU", "Europe", "EMEA"]

[groups]
location = ["country", "state", "city"]
product = ["category", "subcategory", "sku"]

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: Aliases map variant spellings to a canonical form. During diff comparison, all variants are normalized before checking for changes.

docs.title: Inline Aliases
docs.text:
Pass aliases directly in the strategy dict:

import additory as add

diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={
        'aliases': {
            'status': ['Active', 'ACTIVE', 'active'],
            'region': ['NA', 'North America'],
        },
    },
)

The first value in each list becomes the canonical form. So "ACTIVE" and "active" are both normalized to "Active" before comparison.

docs.title: Aliases from a File
docs.text:
Register a reconciliation file, then reference it by name:

# Load reconciliation definitions
add.scan('@set', './reconciliation/')

# Use by name
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'aliases': 'my_reconciliation'},
)

docs.title: How Aliases Work
docs.text:
1. Before comparing rows, the diff engine applies alias normalization
  2. Each column listed in [aliases] has its values mapped to the canonical form
  3. The comparison runs on the normalized values
  4. The output shows the original values (not the normalized ones)

This means a row where old.status = "ACTIVE" and new.status = "active" is reported as no_change rather than modified.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: Groups define column hierarchies for structured change detection. They help answer questions like: "Did the country change, or just the city?"

docs.title: Group Definition
docs.text:
[groups]
location = ["country", "state", "city"]

This defines a hierarchy: country → state → city. When the diff engine detects a change in any of these columns, it reports which level of the hierarchy changed.

docs.title: Using Groups
docs.text:
diff = add.scan('@diff', old=df_old, new=df_new,
    strategy={'groups': 'my_reconciliation'},
)

docs.title: How Groups Work
docs.text:
1. The diff engine checks each group's columns in hierarchy order
  2. If a higher-level column changed (e.g., country), lower-level changes are expected
  3. If only a lower-level column changed (e.g., city), it's flagged as a minor change
  4. This gives you structured visibility into what actually changed

docs.title: The reconciliation file
docs.text:
clinical_reconciliation.add
[aliases]
diagnosis = [
    "Hypertension", "HTN", "High Blood Pressure",
    "Diabetes", "DM", "Diabetes Mellitus",
    "Asthma", "Bronchial Asthma",
]
status = ["Active", "ACTIVE", "active", "Discharged", "DISCHARGED"]

[groups]
location = ["hospital", "ward", "bed"]
treatment = ["department", "procedure", "medication"]

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

# Load reconciliation
add.scan('@set', './reconciliation/')

old_patients = pl.DataFrame({
    'patient_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'diagnosis': ['HTN', 'DM', 'Asthma'],
    'status': ['ACTIVE', 'active', 'Active'],
})

new_patients = pl.DataFrame({
    'patient_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'diagnosis': ['Hypertension', 'Diabetes', 'Bronchial Asthma'],
    'status': ['Active', 'Active', 'Discharged'],
})

# Without reconciliation: 3 rows show as modified
diff_raw = add.scan('@diff', old=old_patients, new=new_patients)

# With reconciliation: only patient 3 shows as modified (status changed)
diff_reconciled = add.scan('@diff', old=old_patients, new=new_patients,
    strategy={'aliases': 'clinical_reconciliation'},
)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common errors, migration steps from older API versions, and Rust binding issues.

docs.title: ImportError: Rust bindings not available
docs.text:
ImportError: add.to() requires Rust bindings.
Install with: pip install additory[rust]

Cause: The compiled Rust extension (_additory) is not installed or not compatible with your Python version.

Fix:

pip install additory --force-reinstall

If building from source:

cd additory
pip install maturin
maturin develop --release

docs.title: ValueError: Cannot use 'as_type' with 'lineage=True'
docs.text:
ValueError: Cannot use 'as_type' with 'lineage=True' in add.to().

Cause: Lineage metadata is stored in the DataFrame's native format and would be lost during type conversion.

Fix: Use one or the other:

# Option 1: Track lineage without type conversion
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', lineage=True)

# Option 2: Convert type without lineage
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id', as_type='polars')

docs.title: TypeError: synthetic() got an unexpected keyword argument 'mode'
docs.text:
TypeError: The 'mode' keyword argument has been removed in v0.1.3a11.

Cause: The add.synthetic() signature changed. The first argument is now df_or_mode, not a separate mode keyword.

Fix:

# Old (broken)
result = add.synthetic(mode='@new', n=100, strategy={...})

# New (correct)
result = add.synthetic('@new', n=100, strategy={...})

docs.title: ValueError: inbuilt: prefix is deprecated
docs.text:
ValueError: The 'inbuilt:' prefix is deprecated. Use expression names directly.

Cause: In @calc mode, the inbuilt: prefix for built-in expressions has been deprecated in favour of direct name resolution.

Fix:

# Old
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='inbuilt:bmi')

# New — still works but may show a warning
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='inbuilt:bmi')

# Or use the dynamic API directly
result = add.bmi(df)

Note

The inbuilt: prefix still works in v0.1.3a11 but raises a migration warning. It may be removed in a future version.

docs.title: Parameter renames in add.to()
docs.text:
Old Name New Name Notes target_df bring_to First positional argument fetch_from bring_from Second positional argument fetch bring Third positional argument by against Fourth positional argument 
# Old
result = add.to(df, fetch_from=ref, fetch=['name'], by='id')

# New
result = add.to(df, ref, 'name', 'id')
# Or with keywords:
result = add.to(bring_to=df, bring_from=ref, bring='name', against='id')

docs.title: add.synthetic() signature change
docs.text:
The first argument changed from mode to df_or_mode:

# Old — mode as keyword
result = add.synthetic(mode='@new', n=100, strategy={...})

# New — mode as positional, or DataFrame for augment
result = add.synthetic('@new', n=100, strategy={...})
result = add.synthetic(df, n=100)  # augment mode inferred

docs.title: add.analyze() → add.scan('@analyze')
docs.text:
# Old (still works as alias)
result = add.analyze(df)

# New (recommended)
result = add.scan('@analyze', df)

docs.title: Tuples → Lists
docs.text:
All list parameters now expect lists, not tuples:

# Old
result = add.to(df, ref, ('name', 'age'), 'id')

# New
result = add.to(df, ref, ['name', 'age'], 'id')

docs.title: From v0.1.3a4 → v0.1.3a5
docs.text:
The by parameter in add.to() was renamed to against:

# Old (v0.1.3a4)
result = add.to(df, fetch_from=ref, fetch=['age'], by='id')

# New (v0.1.3a5+)
result = add.to(df, ref, 'age', 'id')

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
If pip install additory fails to find a pre-built wheel for your platform:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# Install maturin
pip install maturin

# Build from source
cd additory
maturin develop --release

docs.text:
Additory supports Python 3.9 through 3.13. If you're on an older version:

For other platforms, build from source using the steps above.

docs.title: @aggregate
docs.text: Group rows by one or more columns and summarize values using aggregation strategies — sum, count, average, and more.

docs.title: Simple Example

import additory as add
import polars as pl

docs.title: @calc
docs.text: Calculate new columns from expressions — arithmetic, string operations, or built-in formulas from the expression library.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'price': [100, 200, 300],
    'quantity': [2, 3, 1],
})

result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity', name='total')
print(result)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The @calc mode uses these parameters from add.transform():

Parameter Type Default Description expression str or list[str] None Expression(s) to evaluate name str or list[str] None Output column name(s) for the result strategy dict None Map of {name: expression} for multiple columns position str or int 'end' Where to place new columns

docs.title: Single Expression
docs.text:
Use expression and name to calculate one column at a time:

result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity', name='total')

Supported operators: +, -, *, /, ** (power), % (modulo).

# Arithmetic
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='salary * 1.1', name='new_salary')

# String concatenation (when columns are text)
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='first_name + " " + last_name', name='full_name')

docs.title: Using the strategy parameter
docs.text:
The strategy dict maps output column names to expressions. Columns are calculated in order, so later expressions can reference earlier ones:

result = add.transform('@calc', df, strategy={
    'total': 'price * quantity',
    'tax': 'total * 0.1',
    'grand_total': 'total + tax',
})

docs.title: Using lists
docs.text:
Pass parallel lists of expressions and names:

result = add.transform('@calc', df,
    expression=['price * quantity', 'price * 0.1'],
    name=['total', 'discount'],
)

Strategy is cleaner for chained calculations

When later columns depend on earlier ones (like tax depending on total), use the strategy dict. The list form evaluates each expression independently against the original columns.

docs.title: Positioning
docs.text:
Control where new columns appear in the result:

# At the start
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity',
    name='total', position='start')

# After a specific column
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity',
    name='total', position='after:price')

# Before a specific column
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity',
    name='total', position='before:quantity')

# At a specific index
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='price * quantity',
    name='total', position=2)

docs.title: Built-in Expressions
docs.text:
Use the inbuilt: prefix to reference expressions from the built-in library:

# BMI from weight and height columns
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='inbuilt:bmi')

# ROI from revenue and cost columns
result = add.transform('@calc', df, expression='inbuilt:roi')

Built-in expressions auto-match column names from your DataFrame to the expression's required inputs. For example, inbuilt:bmi expects columns named weight and height.

Expression catalog

See the Expression Catalog for the full list of built-in expressions across core, finance, medical, physics, chemistry, engineering, and statistics categories.

docs.title: @deduce
docs.text: Fill missing values using statistical imputation or deduce labels from text similarity. Seven imputation methods handle numeric gaps; TF-IDF handles categorical deduction from text columns.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dave'],
    'age': [25, None, 35, None],
    'salary': [50000, 60000, None, 55000],
})

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='age', method='mean')
print(result)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description infer str or list[str] (required) Column(s) to fill method str or list[str] (required for numeric) Imputation method against str or list[str] None Text column(s) for TF-IDF similarity strategy dict None Advanced options (e.g., KNN parameters) name str None Output column name (defaults to {infer}_infer)

docs.title: mean
docs.text:
Replace missing values with the column mean:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='salary', method='mean')

docs.title: median
docs.text:
Replace missing values with the column median:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='salary', method='median')

docs.title: mode
docs.text:
Replace missing values with the most frequent value:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='department', method='mode')

docs.title: forward_fill
docs.text:
Propagate the last valid value forward:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='temperature', method='forward_fill')

docs.title: backward_fill
docs.text:
Propagate the next valid value backward:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='temperature', method='backward_fill')

docs.title: interpolate
docs.text:
Linear interpolation between known values:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='pressure', method='interpolate')

docs.title: knn
docs.text:
K-nearest neighbors imputation — uses similar rows to estimate missing values:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='age', method='knn')

Configure KNN with the strategy parameter:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='age', method='knn',
    strategy={'k': 5, 'weights': 'distance'},
)
Strategy Key Type Default Description k int 3 Number of neighbors weights str 'uniform' Weighting: 'uniform' or 'distance'

Pure Rust implementation

KNN imputation runs entirely in Rust with support for Euclidean, Manhattan, and Cosine distance metrics. No scikit-learn dependency required.

docs.title: TF-IDF Label Deduction
docs.text:
For categorical columns, use TF-IDF text similarity to deduce missing labels from related text columns:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'description': [
        'Chest pain and shortness of breath',
        'Broken arm from fall',
        'Persistent cough and wheezing',
        'Swollen ankle after running',
    ],
    'category': ['Cardiology', None, 'Pulmonology', None],
})

result = add.transform('@deduce', df, infer='category', against='description')

The engine builds a TF-IDF matrix from the against column(s), finds the most similar rows that have known labels, and assigns those labels to the missing entries.

Multiple text columns

Pass a list to against to combine multiple text columns for similarity: 

result = add.transform('@deduce', df,
    infer='category',
    against=['title', 'description', 'notes'],
)

docs.title: Multiple Columns
docs.text:
Impute several columns at once by passing lists:

result = add.transform('@deduce', df,
    infer=['age', 'salary'],
    method=['mean', 'median'],
)

Each column is paired with its corresponding method.

docs.title: Clinical data cleanup
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

patients = pl.DataFrame({
    'patient_id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    'age': [45, None, 62, None, 38],
    'blood_pressure': [120, 135, None, 128, None],
    'notes': [
        'History of hypertension',
        'Elevated BP readings',
        'Cardiac monitoring',
        'Routine checkup',
        'Young healthy patient',
    ],
    'risk_level': ['High', None, 'High', None, 'Low'],
})

# Numeric imputation
result = add.transform('@deduce', patients, infer='age', method='knn')
result = add.transform('@deduce', result, infer='blood_pressure', method='mean')

# Label deduction from notes
result = add.transform('@deduce', result, infer='risk_level', against='notes')

docs.title: @filter & @sort
docs.text: Filter rows with SQL-like conditions and sort DataFrames by one or more columns.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dave'],
    'age': [25, 17, 30, 15],

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description where str None SQL-like filter condition columns str or list[str] None Select specific columns in the output

docs.title: Filter Conditions
docs.text:
The where parameter accepts SQL-like expressions:

# Comparison operators
result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='age >= 18')
result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='salary > 50000')
result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='status == "active"')

result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='phone is null')

result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='name == "Alice"')

docs.text:

# Select columns only
result = add.transform('@filter', df, columns=['name', 'age'])

# Filter rows AND select columns
result = add.transform('@filter', df, where='age >= 18', columns=['name', 'department'])

Provide your own exchange rates for currency conversion:

result = add.transform('@harmonize', df, columns='price',
    strategy={'from': 'USD', 'to': 'EUR', 'rate': 0.92})

No built-in exchange rates

Currency conversion requires a user-provided rate in the strategy. Additory does not fetch live exchange rates (no internet access by design).

docs.title: Multiple Columns
docs.text:
Convert several columns at once:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'height_in': [68.0, 72.0, 65.0],
    'weight_lbs': [150.0, 180.0, 130.0],
})

result = add.transform('@harmonize', df, columns=['height_in', 'weight_lbs'],
    strategy={'from': ['in', 'lbs'], 'to': ['cm', 'kg']})

docs.title: International data standardization
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

us_data = pl.DataFrame({
    'city': ['New York', 'Chicago', 'Phoenix'],
    'temp_f': [75.0, 68.0, 105.0],
    'distance_mi': [12.5, 8.3, 15.7],

# Convert to metric
result = add.transform('@harmonize', us_data, columns='temp_f',
    strategy={'from': 'F', 'to': 'C'})
result = add.transform('@harmonize', result, columns='distance_mi',
    strategy={'from': 'mi', 'to': 'km'})

docs.title: Text Modes
docs.text: Four transform modes for working with text and categorical data: extract patterns, split columns, one-hot encode, and label encode.

docs.title: @extract
docs.text: Pull patterns or datetime components out of text columns.

docs.title: Pattern Extraction
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'email': ['alice@example.com', 'bob@company.org', 'carol@test.net'],
})

result = add.transform('@extract', df, columns='email', expression=r'@(\w+)')
print(result)

docs.title: Datetime Extraction
docs.text:
Extract year, month, day, or other components from datetime columns:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'created_at': ['2026-01-15', '2026-03-22', '2026-07-04'],
})

result = add.transform('@extract', df, columns='created_at', expression='year')

Available datetime components: year, month, day, hour, minute, second, weekday.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description columns str or list[str] Column(s) to extract from expression str Regex pattern or datetime component name

docs.title: @split
docs.text:
Split a text column into multiple columns based on a separator.

import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'full_name': ['Alice Smith', 'Bob Jones', 'Carol Lee'],
})

result = add.transform('@split', df, columns='full_name', by=' ')
print(result)

This creates columns full_name_0, full_name_1, etc.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description columns str or list[str] (required) Column(s) to split by str (required) Separator string

docs.title: @onehot
docs.text:
One-hot encode categorical columns into binary indicator columns.

import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'color': ['red', 'blue', 'green', 'red', 'blue'],
    'size': ['S', 'M', 'L', 'M', 'S'],
})

result = add.transform('@onehot', df, columns='color')
print(result)

This creates columns like color_red, color_blue, color_green with values 1 or 0.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description columns str or list[str] Column(s) to one-hot encode

docs.title: @label
docs.text:
Label encode categorical columns into numeric values.

import additory as add
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    'status': ['active', 'inactive', 'pending', 'active', 'inactive'],
})

result = add.transform('@label', df, columns='status')
print(result)

Each unique value gets a numeric label (e.g., active → 0, inactive → 1, pending → 2). The original column is preserved and a new {column}_label column is added.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description columns str or list[str] Column(s) to label encode

docs.title: Preparing text data for analysis
docs.text:
import additory as add
import polars as pl

survey = pl.DataFrame({
    'response': ['Very Satisfied', 'Satisfied', 'Neutral', 'Dissatisfied', 'Very Satisfied'],
    'comment': ['Great service at NYC office', 'Good experience in LA', 'OK visit to CHI branch'],
})

# Label encode the ordinal response
result = add.transform('@label', survey, columns='response')

# Extract city abbreviations from comments
result = add.transform('@extract', result, columns='comment', expression=r'\b[A-Z]{2,3}\b')

docs.text:
products = pl.DataFrame({
    'sku': ['ELEC-001-US', 'FOOD-042-UK', 'ELEC-007-DE'],
    'category': ['Electronics', 'Food', 'Electronics'],

# Split SKU into components

# One-hot encode category
result = add.transform('@onehot', result, columns='category')
